paras: The killing of Stephen Allchin was the shooting death of Stephen W. Allchin in front of a store at Hempstead, Waller County, Texas, on May 19, 1888, by Deputy Sheriff Dick Springfield and Jack McDade. Both men were charged with murder and refused bail, and the state sent Texas Rangers to Hempstead to keep order and protect witnesses. Texas papers called the killing an "assassination" and described a "reign of terror" in Waller County.

According to the Atlanta Constitution, the trouble began when the Hempstead Guard printed an article criticizing county officers, including the sheriff, and Allchin was named as its author. On April 4, 1888, Allchin and Deputy Sheriff Richard C. Chambers met and opened fire, and Chambers was killed while Allchin was badly wounded.

About 11 o'clock on the morning of Saturday, May 19, Allchin rode up in front of Harmon's store and sat on his horse. Jack McDade and Dick Springfield came around the back of the store and shot him, "it is said, without warning," with a shotgun and a six-shooter, killing him instantly. On Sunday, May 20, Lincoln Lodge No. 35 of the Ancient Order of United Workmen buried him, and a Hempstead correspondent called it the largest funeral ever seen in the town.

The two men were held as prisoners, and when Adjutant-General King visited Hempstead on May 22 he found them barricaded in the courthouse with Sheriff McDade, who refused to come and see him. On May 23 he ordered Captain McMurray and about ten rangers to Hempstead to protect citizens and prevent intimidation of witnesses.

On May 24 a mass meeting of about 500 Waller County citizens asked Governor L. S. Ross to act for "the enforcement of the laws and protection of life" and voted to petition Sheriff Thomas S. McDade to resign, a petition 108 leading citizens signed. The examining trial opened May 29 with rangers guarding the courtroom and searching everyone who entered. The prosecution rested May 31, and on June 4 Justice R. M. Thornton ruled the case not bailable after District Attorney Hannay's closing argument.

The Court of Appeals upheld the denial of bail on June 27. Over the summer the prisoners were kept away from Hempstead, in the Galveston jail by one report, and the Austin Statesman said their removal was kept secret for fear "of a rescue by friends of the prisoners." They returned to the district court at Hempstead on September 4 under ranger guard, and by late November both were under indictment. Former Sheriff McDade was himself shot dead from ambush on November 26, and a young Blossingame who lived at the Allchin place was arrested on suspicion. About forty witnesses left for Houston on December 12 for the trial set there the next day; no report of its result appears in the coverage.

Coverage came almost entirely from Texas papers, led by the Fort Worth Daily Gazette's Hempstead and Austin correspondents and the Austin Statesman's special telegrams. These papers called the accused "the assassins" and "the Hempstead murderers," headlined the bail ruling "The Hempstead Horror," and wrote that the ruling would end "the reign of terror and bloodshed, which has so long disgraced Waller county." After the appeals ruling the Gazette's Austin correspondent wrote, "Unless they can get a negro jory it looks now like Springfield and McDade will hang in the near future."

Outside Texas, the Atlanta Constitution ran a letter headed "Trouble at Hempstead" that traced the killing to a newspaper article and repeated the claim that Allchin had threatened the deputy. In September a Statesman editorial on a Brenham murder called the Allchin killing "a fearful, bloody and cowardly crime" but noted it was done in daylight with no attempt at concealment.

The Atlanta Constitution's letter differs from the same-day Hempstead report: it says Allchin was shot in the back of the head while driving his buggy, by one deputy, with "Jack McLean, a son of the sheriff" present. The same letter said the sheriff called out militia "to prevent mob law," while Adjutant-General King reported that leading citizens had "no intention of resorting to lynch law."

reader.title: Killing of Stephen Allchin
bases: Two named men, a deputy sheriff and the sheriff's young relative, shot Allchin on a town street in what the papers tie to an earlier feud with the sheriff's office; no mob, band or posse did the killing, and the crowd element was only the public excitement that brought out militia and rangers (A4, A7, A8).

A Hempstead report the day of the killing (A4), an Austin dispatch (A7), an out-of-state letter (A8) and the court record of the examining trial and bail rulings (A10, A14, A15) agree that Springfield and Jack McDade were charged with shooting Allchin dead at Hempstead.
